name: Empiricism
statement: Knowledge comes from experience: the mind begins as a blank slate written on by the senses.
statementAccent: the mind begins as a blank slate
meaning: Empiricism is the epistemological view that knowledge, and the concepts we use, derives primarily or entirely from sense experience, observation, and the senses, rather than from reason or innate ideas. The empiricist thesis is that we have no source of knowledge, or of the concepts we employ, other than experience, and empiricists therefore emphasize evidence, especially as gained through the senses and through experiment, as the basis of knowledge. Central to the view is the rejection of innate ideas: all our concepts derive ultimately from experience, and the mind at birth is, in John Locke's famous image, a blank slate, a tabula rasa, written on by experience. Empiricism is most associated with the British Empiricists, Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume, though it has ancient roots in Aristotle and the maxim that there is nothing in the intellect that was not first in the senses, and a modern methodological champion in Francis Bacon, who urged the inductive, experimental study of nature. Empiricism stands in classic opposition to rationalism, the view of Descartes, Spinoza, and Leibniz that reason is a source of knowledge independent of experience and that some ideas are innate. In the twentieth century, logical empiricism, or logical positivism, gave the tradition a new form. The rationalism and empiricism debate is central to early modern philosophy and to the theory of knowledge.
mechanism: Empiricism derives knowledge and concepts from experience, and its classic figures worked out how. John Locke argued that the mind begins as a blank slate and that all its materials come from two sources of experience: sensation, the input of the external senses, and reflection, the mind's awareness of its own operations; there are no innate ideas or principles, and even complex ideas are built up from simple ones given in experience. George Berkeley pushed empiricism toward idealism, holding that to be is to be perceived, that the objects of knowledge are ideas and that there is no material substance existing unperceived behind them. David Hume gave the tradition its most rigorous and skeptical development, distinguishing impressions, the vivid, direct deliverances of experience, from ideas, their fainter copies in thought, and insisting that every legitimate idea must be traceable to some impression; on this basis he argued that we never observe necessary causal connection but only the constant conjunction of events, so that our idea of causation reflects a habit of mind rather than something read off from experience, and he framed the problem of induction. Across these thinkers the mechanism is the same: trace concepts back to their experiential origins, admit as knowledge only what experience can support, and reject appeals to innate ideas or to reason operating independently of the senses. Logical empiricism later added the verification principle, that a statement is cognitively meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable.

examples.text: Locke held the mind begins as a tabula rasa, furnished only by experience through sensation and reflection.
Hume distinguished vivid impressions from their fainter copies, ideas, insisting every idea trace back to some impression.
Hume argued we never observe necessary causal connection, only the constant conjunction of events, making causation a habit of mind.

variants.name: British empiricism
variants.text: The tradition of Locke, Berkeley, and Hume grounding knowledge in sense experience and rejecting innate ideas.

variants.name: Logical empiricism
variants.text: The twentieth-century Vienna Circle view that meaningful statements are either analytic or empirically verifiable.

whyItMatters: Empiricism is one of the two great traditions in the theory of knowledge, the rival and complement to rationalism, and it underlies the modern scientific outlook. By insisting that knowledge comes from experience, observation, and experiment rather than from pure reason or innate ideas, empiricism gave philosophical expression to the experimental method and shaped the way we think about evidence, testing, and the authority of observation. The British Empiricists, Locke, Berkeley, and Hume, produced some of the most influential works in the history of philosophy, and Hume's analysis of causation and his problem of induction pose challenges that philosophy of science still grapples with. Locke's tabula rasa reframed debates about the mind, human nature, and even politics and education. In the twentieth century, logical empiricism sought to make the empiricist standard precise through the verification principle, with lasting influence on the philosophy of science even as the principle itself ran into trouble. The rationalism and empiricism debate culminated in Kant's attempt to synthesize the two.

working.text: hold that all knowledge and concepts derive from sense experience, observation, and reflection.
treat the mind as a blank slate furnished by experience, denying innate ideas and principles.
admit as knowledge what experience and experiment can support, tracing ideas back to their origins.

limits: Empiricism faces powerful objections, several first raised from within the tradition by Hume. The problem of induction, which Hume himself pressed, holds that empirical generalizations from observed to unobserved cases cannot be rationally justified, since any such inference presupposes the uniformity of nature, which can itself be supported only inductively, on pain of circularity. A second difficulty is a priori knowledge: the truths of mathematics and logic appear to be known independently of experience, and to be necessary and universal in a way that mere observation could never establish, which strict empiricism struggles to accommodate. Rationalists press that some concepts, such as causation or substance, seem to outrun anything the senses supply. And the logical empiricists' verification principle turned out to be self-refuting, since the principle itself is neither analytic nor empirically verifiable, so by its own standard it is meaningless, and it also seemed too restrictive, since universal scientific laws are not conclusively verifiable.
misreadings: Empiricism is not the claim that reason plays no role in knowledge; it holds that the materials of knowledge come from experience, while granting reason a role in combining and reasoning about them. It is not committed to naive certainty about the senses, since Hume's empiricism is deeply skeptical, raising the problem of induction and questioning causation. And Locke's tabula rasa is a claim about the origin of ideas, not a denial of native capacities of mind, so treating empiricism as anti-rational, as complacently confident, or as denying all innate faculties, misreads a foundational epistemological tradition.
origin: The epistemological tradition holding that knowledge and concepts derive from sense experience rather than reason or innate ideas, developed by the British Empiricists Locke, Berkeley, and Hume and later by the logical empiricists.
